@Sébastien Gouëzel do you understand why

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.VectorBundle.Riemannian

open Bundle

variable
  {M : Type*} {V : M → Type*}
  [∀ x, AddCommGroup (V x)] [∀ x, Module ℝ (V x)]
  [∀ x : M, TopologicalSpace (V x)]
  [∀ x, IsTopologicalAddGroup (V x)] [∀ x, ContinuousSMul ℝ (V x)]
  [RiemannianBundle V]

variable {σ σ' : Π x : M, V x}

set_option trace.profiler true

#check fun x : M ↦ inner ℝ (σ x) (σ' x)

takes forever?
This is pretty noticeable when it impacts every declaration in #36299 for instance.
What other instances does it try before going to the priority 80 instance Bundle.instInnerProductSpaceReal?

First trace level is

[Elab.command] [1.234402] #check fun x : M ↦ inner ℝ (σ x) (σ' x) ▼
  [step] [0.017410] expected type: Sort ?u.88845, term
      ∀ x, Module ℝ (V x) ▶
  [step] [0.429708] expected type: Sort ?u.89699, term
      ∀ x, IsTopologicalAddGroup (V x) ▶
  [step] [0.314358] expected type: Sort ?u.119568, term
      ∀ x, ContinuousSMul ℝ (V x) ▶
  [step] [0.464675] expected type: <not-available>, term
      fun x : M ↦ inner ℝ (σ x) (σ' x) ▶
So it’s not even the inner product that seems to bring trouble.
It already takes almost half a second to find ∀ (x : M), IsTopologicalAddGroup (V x) which is a local variable, and same for ContinuousSmul.
And I don’t even know why Lean is looking for this!
I mean I understand the instance you mention looks for this, but I don’t understand why we need this to talk about inner product on the fibers of a fiber bundle.

Anatole Dedecker said:

Aah yes apologies, I have incorrectly claimed that we triumphantly unbundled topology from algebra more than once. I've edited my post. I confuse it with the successful extraction of the order hierarchy from the algebra hierarchy in #20676 which resulted in a massive speed-up of mathlib.

Is it time to extract the norm hierarchy from the algebra hierarchy?

Last I heard, unbundling the norm hierarchy from algebra was blocked by a change to lean 4, right? #PR reviews > #28803 refactor: unbundle algebra from `ENormed*`. Maybe it's worth pushing for that a bit harder or spending time discussing if we can move forward without it?

I'd have to take a closer look at the results, and probably re-do them to make sure it is up to date.
Sure. Many things have changed since then.

@Sébastien Gouëzel yes I remember your work here and I should have noted that this had already been tried. What prompted my outburst above was that I was thinking that maybe we've now found the reason for unbundling. We didn't unbundle order from algebra in 2018 because it wasn't a problem , it only became a problem later. Or do you think my instinct is wrong and there's nothing new here so your instinct is that unbundling will continue to not help?

The issue, as far as I can tell, is that many things depend on a given nontrivially normed field. The moment you unbundle this one, then they depend on a field with a norm, a topology, and some interaction between all these. Depending on the various bundling you try, this goes from one class to 2, 3 or 4 classes. And nontrivially normed fields are so ubiquitous in definitions (of derivatives, of spaces of continuous linear maps, and so on) that the complexity in these definitions blows up, not making it up for the gain in typeclass inference.

@Michael Rothgang, can you try with

attribute [instance 850] NormedAddGroup.toAddGroup SeminormedAddGroup.toAddGroup
  NormedAlgebra.toAlgebra ESeminormedAddMonoid.toAddMonoid ESeminormedAddCommMonoid.toAddCommMonoid

to see if it helps? It does in my test file, but I'd be interested to know how much you gain in real life conditions.
I won't be at my computer in the next week (holidays), but feel free to push that change to #36299 yourself. (There is already a performance hack; this could replace or extend it.)

Also, there is an issue with the phrasing of assumptions in #36299, mostly orthogonal to the slowness question but using the right phrasing will probably make things better. You are assuming RiemannianBundle V, but that's not a good idea. It's a data-carrying class to put an inner product space structure on the fibers of a vector bundle that already have a topological space structure (so, useful for the tangent bundle typically). The better wording would be

{V : M → Type*} [TopologicalSpace (TotalSpace F V)]
  [∀ x, NormedAddCommGroup (V x)] [∀ x, InnerProductSpace ℝ (V x)]
  [FiberBundle F V] [VectorBundle ℝ F V] [IsContinuousRiemannianBundle F V]

All this is explained in the file-level docstring of Mathlib.Topology.VectorBundle.Riemannian. But if you got confused this is certainly an indication that the explanations are not clear enough, and that we should explain this in the docstring of docs#Bundle.RiemannianBundle.

I have started investigating the root issue. To me, it looks like a Lean issue with caching during typeclass inference for Pi types (due to the fact that pi types are not indexed?). In the trace, I get

[1.107784] ❌️ apply @SeminormedAddCommGroup.toIsTopologicalAddGroup to ∀ (b : M), IsTopologicalAddGroup (V b) ▼

and inside the search for this one I get

[0.752844] ❌️ apply @SeminormedAddCommGroup.toIsTopologicalAddGroup to ∀ (b : M), IsTopologicalAddGroup (V b) ▼

(exactly the same goal) -- and inside the search for this one I get

[0.398899] ❌️ apply @SeminormedAddCommGroup.toIsTopologicalAddGroup to ∀ (b : M), IsTopologicalAddGroup (V b) ▼

(exactly the same goal) - and inside the search for this one I get, guess what,

[0.049559] ❌️ apply @SeminormedAddCommGroup.toIsTopologicalAddGroup to ∀ (b : M), IsTopologicalAddGroup (V b) ▼

Does it ring a bell? (Even with pp.all, the goals are exactly identical, and they don't contain any metavariable)

To reproduce:

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.VectorBundle.Riemannian

open Bundle

variable
  {M : Type} {V : M → Type}
  [∀ x, AddCommGroup (V x)] [∀ x, Module ℝ (V x)]
  [∀ x : M, TopologicalSpace (V x)]

variable {x : M}

set_option trace.profiler true
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true

#synth AddGroup (V x)
Each new call seems to happen in a isDefEq call for the previous one.

I have a #mwe:

class SGTop (α : Type)
class SGIsCont (α : Type) [SGTop α]
class SGNormed (α : Type) extends SGTop α

instance {α : Type} [SGNormed α] : SGIsCont α where

class SGBundle {β : Type} (α : β → Type) [∀ x, SGTop (α x)]

instance {β : Type} {α : β → Type} [∀ x, SGTop (α x)] [∀ x, SGIsCont (α x)] [SGBundle α] (b : β) :
    SGNormed (α b) where

variable {β : Type} {α : β → Type} [∀ x, SGTop (α x)]

set_option trace.profiler true
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true

#synth ∀ b, SGIsCont (α b)

gives somewhere inside the instance trace the following

      [] [0.004335] ❌️ (b : β) → SGNormed (α b) ▼
        [] [0.000020] new goal (b : β) → SGNormed (α b) ▶
        [] [0.000559] ✅️ apply @instSGNormedOfSGIsContOfSGBundle to (b : β) → SGNormed (α b) ▶
        [] [0.000156] ✅️ apply inst✝ to (x : β) → SGTop (α x) ▶
        [resume] [0.000038] propagating (x : β) → SGTop (α x) to subgoal (x : β) → SGTop (α x) of (b : β) → SGNormed (α b) ▶
        [resume] [0.000049] propagating β → (x : β) → SGTop (α x) to subgoal β → (x : β) → SGTop (α x) of (b : β) → SGNormed (α b) ▶
        [] [0.003351] ✅️ apply @instSGIsCont to (x : β) → SGIsCont (α x) ▼
          [tryResolve] [0.003304] ✅️ SGIsCont (α x) ≟ SGIsCont (α x) ▼
            [] [0.002974] ❌️ (x : β) → SGNormed (α x) ▶

On the first line, it's trying to synthetize an SGNormed instance. To do this, it tries to applies some instance, and at some point it needs an SGNormed instance (the one we started with). Instead of stopping and saying we're looping, it tries to get it, by the same process.

In fact it's not related to Pi types, it's related to maxSynthPendingDepth (which measures the number of loops before one stops). So probably the cache is not shared well enough between different depths (or loops are not detected between different depths). Here is a better example, without Pi types:

class SGTop (α : Type)
class SGIsCont (α : Type) [SGTop α]
class SGNormed (α : Type) extends SGTop α
class SGBundle (α : Type) [SGTop α]

instance instIsContOfNormed {α : Type} [SGNormed α] : SGIsCont α where
instance instIsNormedOfBundle {α : Type} [SGTop α] [SGIsCont α] [SGBundle α] : SGNormed α where

variable {α : Type} [SGTop α]

set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 500

/--
error: failed to synthesize
  SGNormed α
maximum recursion depth has been reached
use `set_option maxRecDepth <num>` to increase limit
use `set_option diagnostics true` to get diagnostic information

Hint: Additional diagnostic information may be available using the `set_option diagnostics true` command.
-/
#guard_msgs in
#synth SGIsCont α

To synthetize SGIsCont, Lean tries to deduced it from SGNormed through instIsContOfNormed. To get the normed structure, it tries to apply instIsNormedOfBundle. But for this it needs SGIsCont -- except that the depth is one more, so it doesn't detect the loop, and goes on forever until the max depth is reached.

Has anyone already seen this? Otherwise, I'll report it to core.

It looks like it is hitting the maxSynthPendingDepth due to a recursion. This isn't meant to happen, and there is no cache that detects this. The cache only exists "on one level", so a nested type class search (that is invoked during a unification step of the outer type class search) does not share the cache with the outer type class search.
Yes, that's the issue, that cache are not shared at different levels. Here it creates a loop.

For the case at hand, I improve the situation in #37028 (by changing the order of parameters in some instance). But it is not completely satisfactory (the loop can still happen in some specific situations).

Indeed, instNormedAddCommGroupOfRiemannianBundle seems to be a bad instance here, because it has IsTopologicalAddGroup as a subgoals for synthesizing NormedAddCommGroup. Maybe this is a quirk of the fact that topological add groups are unbundled, while normed add groups are bundled?

Normally this shouldn't be a problem because loops in typeclass inference are supposed to be safe. Here it's only an issue because of the depth. Putting IsTopologicalAddGroup after RiemannianBundle in the instance order solves most of the issues, though.

But do you understand why cache shouldn't be shared at different depths? When at depth n+1, couldn't one start with the cache of depth n, and in the end discard all the changes once one is done with step n+1 and goes back to depth n?

When type class search applies an instance, it does unification. And in your example, the unification cannot succeed unless the instance has already been synthesized, so unification calls a fresh new type class search that is independent from the original type class search.

This is different from "normal" type class search loops, where the unification succeeds, and then type class search continues like normal, with its cache.

In particular, in your example

class SGTop (α : Type)
class SGIsCont (α : Type) [SGTop α]
class SGNormed (α : Type) extends SGTop α

instance instIsContOfNormed {α : Type} [SGNormed α] : SGIsCont α where
instance instIsNormedOfBundle {α : Type} [SGTop α] [SGIsCont α] : SGNormed α where

variable {α : Type} [SGTop α]

set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 500
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true
set_option trace.Meta.isDefEq true
set_option pp.explicit true

#synth SGIsCont α

The following unification is tricky

[isDefEq] 💥️ @SGIsCont α inst✝ =?= @SGIsCont ?m.3 (@SGNormed.toSGTop ?m.3 ?m.4)

Sure. But why shouldn't typeclass searches during the unification use the existing cache if it can prove useful? After all, everything (without metavariables) that has already been established or dismissed is still valid, right?

One reason is that type class search maintains the invariant that the local context always stays the same, while unification is allowed to introduce new variable to the local context. Of course in this example, the local context isn't changed, but it could in general.
Reported at lean4#13063.
Can you modify your MWE by removing SGBundle? It is not needed for the minimal example.
Done. It's less realistic in a sense, because one would never write such an instance, but it's indeed enough to capture the bad behavior.
Thanks a lot for those investigations!

In practice, I have pushed a change to the PR #36299 on metric connections that fixes everything by changing the typeclass assumptions. And, in parallel, #37028 should work around the bug by changing the order of parameters in some instances (ready for review)

#37962 helps speed things up here. In that PR I lower the priority of some normed instances. So now, when looking for a Monoid/AddMonoid/Group/AddGroup instance, instead of wasting our time searching for e.g. NormedGroup, we first search through the algebraic hierarchy.

I'm not so sure that this is something to celebrate. I think that (a) the PR (now merged) is a hack (b) there are several more places in the library where we could reduce the priority of these instances to get speed-ups and (c) the correct thing to do is to disentangle the norm and algebra heirarchies (ie IsNormedGroup not NormedGroup) but then (d) the analysts will complain that their variable lists will get even longer so they prefer to celebrate hacks.
I think we need to take the complaints by the analysts seriously.

To continue the spicy takes: I think that there are places in the library where we increase instance priority and this is good code design. This is promoting instances which are typically quick to fail and always the right one if they don't. However I'm beginning to wonder whether all of those Note: see reduced instance priority notes in mathlib are hacks. Why are we reducing instance priorities? Because we know they cause trouble! In fact we'd rather they were not there at all but we're kind of stuck with them so we turn them down in the hope that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. I think they're a code smell.

I don't think so. The idea was that instances that are specific should be tried before general instances, so general instances (that always apply) should have lower priority. For instance, if your type has a specific form MyFoo ..., then instances that are specific to MyFoo are very likely to be the right one, so they should be tried first. That's exactly what this reduced instance priority note is about, and it definitely makes sense.

Oh -- looking at the PR on my computer rather than my phone, I do at least now realise that the priority is lowered throughout mathlib, so my comment "I bet there are other places where we can do this" is in error -- if we're going to do it at all then we've done it in the right place. At least this makes me feel a bit better about this hackPR.

But it's the very fact that we have to lower these things at all which makes me think that they should not even be there. Yes they apply in far too many cases. Your argument is "and that's why they should have low priority" but this doesn't stop them applying. My argument is that they shouldn't be there at all and we know exactly how to design things so that they are not there.

Typically, a class like AddGroup has multiple instances that always apply, such as AddCommGroup.toAddGroup, AddGroupWithOne.toAddGroup and NormedAddGroup.toAddGroup. And it matters a lot which one of these is tried first, because of the depth-first-search nature of type class search: If you try one that will fail, it will typically take a long time until you can try another one.

So I would say that explicitly telling Lean our preferences of what order to try these instances in is very reasonable.

@Kevin Buzzard , as I've already told you at least twice, I've already made the experiment where we separate norms from the algebraic hierarchy, and the outcome was worse than the current situation :-)

Yes I remember you told me this :-/ (indeed I was tempted to say "didn't you try this already?"). But here there is evidence that it's the right idea. I am worried that as this part of mathlib increases it might become the case that the current situation is worse then the refactor.
